desc:
Find the longest subsequence of nums that is strictly increasing and in which every two neighbouring chosen elements differ by at most k. In other words, for consecutive chosen values u then v we need 0 < v - u ≤ k.

Return its length. For nums = [4, 2, 1, 4, 3, 4, 5, 8, 15] and k = 3 the answer is 5 (1, 3, 4, 5, 8).
hints: Let best[i] be the longest valid subsequence that ends exactly at index i. Which earlier values can precede nums[i]?

A predecessor must have a value in the range [nums[i] - k, nums[i] - 1]. So best[i] = 1 + the largest best[j] among earlier indices whose value lies in that range. The direct scan is O(n<sup>2</sup>).

Keep a structure indexed by value that stores the best length of a subsequence ending with that value, and supports 'maximum over a range of values' plus 'raise one entry'. A segment tree on the compressed values gives O(log n) per element.
editorial: Plain LIS only needs 'the largest length among smaller values', a prefix maximum that a tails array or Fenwick tree answers. Here the allowed predecessors form a window of values [x - k, x - 1], which is not a prefix, so we need a range maximum query.

Index a segment tree by value (compressed to the sorted distinct values). The entry at value v stores the best length of a valid subsequence processed so far that ends with v. For each element x in order, query the maximum over values in [x - k, x - 1], set cur = 1 + that maximum, and raise the entry of x to at least cur. Equal values do not interact because the query window excludes x itself, and since elements are processed left to right, everything in the tree comes from earlier indices.

The answer is the largest cur seen. Time is O(n log n) with an iterative segment tree, memory O(n). The O(n2) double loop would be too slow for large inputs in an interview setting, which is why the range structure is the heart of the problem.
